content: Efforts were made to establish systems and provide training to various community actors, including traditional birth attendants (TBAs), to enhance awareness of available health services and reproductive health issues. Community outreach and input were prioritized, with each refugee camp forming a health committee comprising community representatives and health service staff. These committees convened bi-monthly to discuss project activities and provide feedback to health workers regarding the services offered. Basic emergency obstetric care facilities were established, and community-based education was delivered to key community representatives, including community health workers (CHWs), female health workers, women of reproductive age, men, health committee members (all men), teachers, religious leaders, and private practitioners. Financial access to care was facilitated for the poor, and village midwives were encouraged to collaborate with TBAs. Maternity care services were culturally adapted to meet local needs. In India, a one-group preand post-evaluation study in 2008 in rural Andhra Pradesh (Rangareddy district) involved village meetings and community activities to increase demand for quality pregnancy-related services. The intervention included raising awareness and fostering community support for pregnant women through local government and youth committees. Families, particularly husbands, were engaged in pregnancy-related care through monthly meetings, and bi-monthly home visits by community organizers helped families create birth preparedness plans and access care. Local government members held regular meetings to review the performance of public health providers and facilities, with representatives of local organizations invited to participate. In Indonesia's West Java in 2004, a preand post-comparative study with a control group implemented social mobilization campaigns. The Suami SIAGA (Alert Husband) campaign used mass media to encourage husbands to be prepared for childbirth, while the Warga SIAGA campaign mobilized community members to support birth preparedness. The Bidan SIAGA campaign promoted midwives as the preferred maternal healthcare providers. In Nepal, a one-group preand post-evaluation study in 2004 in rural districts (Baglung and Lalitpur) employed the SUMATA strategy, a multimedia behavioral change campaign targeting husbands and mothers-in-law to improve maternal health outcomes. In Zimbabwe, maternity waiting homes (MWHs) were established in 1998 on the premises of four out of five hospitals in Mberengwa district, covering 22 clinics offering maternity services. In Chimanimani district in 1996, an MWH close to the hospital provided free accommodation in a simple house with shared rooms, toilets, and showers. Firewood and water were supplied, while women brought their own food and utensils. Women stayed during the last month of pregnancy and were transferred to the hospital if complications arose or labor began. In Eritrea in 2011, a quasi-experimental preand post-study with a non-equivalent control group trained community members (both women and men) to become maternal health volunteers and lead participatory education sessions using developed materials. Skills training for healthcare providers was also conducted, emphasizing birth preparedness and male involvement. In India in 2008, a case study utilized a detailed verbal autopsy questionnaire to identify gaps in officially recorded data, reconstruct the sequence of events, and determine the exact cause of maternal deaths. In Zimbabwe's Gutu district in 1999, a household-level cross-sectional survey was conducted, though no intervention description was provided. In Zambia's Eastern Province in 2003, an MWH next to the maternity ward accommodated 10–15 women, primarily those with high-risk pregnancies referred during the last weeks of pregnancy. The hospital provided food for women at the MWH and charged $3 for those staying in the MWH compared to $6 for those who did not. In Timor-Leste in 2012, small MWHs were established next to facilities in rural areas (Lautem and Manufahi). These homes lacked kitchens or family sleeping spaces, and all women stayed together in a large room with food provided. Women who gave birth in the facility utilized the MWH, and childbirth facilities were relocated to the MWH. This report summarizes the final recommendations and the process for developing guidelines on the effectiveness of health promotion interventions for maternal and newborn health.
